exercises.title: Counting Puffins

exercises.title: Why Onions Make Us Cry
exercises.text:

As {{3}} as this gas reaches your eyes, it reacts with the water in them to form a mild acid. Your eyes then produce tears in order {{4}} wash it away. In other words, crying is your body's way of protecting {{5}}.

Over the years, people have come up {{6}} all kinds of tricks to prevent this. Interestingly, not {{11}} onions are equally strong. Sweet onions contain far less of the chemical {{12}} ordinary ones, and researchers in New Zealand have even developed a 'tearless' variety. {{13}} everyone is pleased. 'Half the fun of cooking {{14}} the drama,' says chef Rosa Pinter. 'If I'm not in tears, nobody believes I've done {{15}} work.'

exercises.title: The Language of Flowers
exercises.text:
Imagine feeling insulted by a bunch of yellow roses. In Victorian England, {{0}} could easily have happened. In {{1}} days, flowers were used to send secret messages, and every plant had {{2}} own meaning. Yellow roses suggested jealousy, for example, while a red tulip was nothing {{3}} than a declaration of love.

A flower that meant 'I adore you' in one book might mean 'Leave me alone' in another, {{9}} must have led to some awkward misunderstandings. The way the flowers were presented mattered, {{10}}. {{11}} a bouquet was offered with the right hand, the answer was 'yes'; if it was offered with the left, it was 'no'.

Although few people today know {{12}} about this secret code, traces of it survive. We still give red roses on Valentine's Day, {{13}} though most of us have no idea why. So before you buy flowers, it might be worth checking what they mean first, just {{14}} case you are saying something you would rather {{15}}!

exercises.text:
